title: Network Delay Time
statement: A network has n nodes numbered 1 to n. Each entry [u, v, w] says a signal sent from u reaches v after w time units, in that direction only. A signal starts at node k. Return how long until every node has received it, or -1 if some node never does.

example.caption: The signal starts at node 1. Node 3 is faster through node 2 (2 + 1) than directly (6). The last node to hear it is 5, at time 6.

output.label: earliest time for nodes 1 to 5. Answer = the largest

idea.sentence: Always finish the unfinished node with the smallest known time next, because no later route can beat it when every link takes zero or more time.

jargon.plain: Shortest paths from one start. Repeatedly take the closest unfinished node, then see if it gives its neighbours a shorter route.
An old heap item whose time is worse than one found later. It cannot be removed from the middle of the heap cheaply, so you skip it when it comes out.
Check whether going through this node gives a neighbour a smaller time. If so, update it.

watch.inputHint: Three arguments: the links [[u,v,w],...], the node count n, the start k. E.g. [[2,1,1],[2,3,1],[3,4,1]], 4, 2

compare.bruteLabel: Scan for the closest node each round

rows.name: Plain array scan
rows.note: Each round scans every node to find the smallest time. Fine for dense graphs.

rows.name: Dijkstra with a heap
rows.note: Each improvement pushes one entry. Each push and pop costs log of the heap size.

rows.name: Bellman-Ford
rows.note: Not shown. Repeats all links V-1 times. Slower, but it also copes with negative weights.

fast.takeaway: The heap hands you the closest unfinished node cheaply. Stale entries are the price: skip them when popped.

stages.title: Start at the source
stages.note: Distance to k is 0, everything else is infinity. Push (0, k) onto a min-heap.

stages.title: Pop the closest
stages.note: Take the smallest time from the heap. If it is older than the best known time, skip it. Otherwise that node is finished.

stages.title: Relax its links
stages.note: For each link out of the finished node, see if the route through it is shorter. If yes, update and push.

stages.title: Answer
stages.note: The slowest node decides the total time. If any node is still infinity, return -1.

edges.title: Node never reached
edges.why: Node 3 has no incoming link, so its distance stays infinity. Check for that before returning the maximum.

edges.title: Only the source
edges.why: The source hears the signal at time 0 and there is no one else to wait for.

edges.title: Direction matters
edges.why: A link from 1 to 2 does not carry signals from 2 to 1. Start at 2 and node 1 is out of reach.

edges.title: Short route found later
edges.why: Node 2 first gets time 10, then 2 through node 3. The 10 entry is still in the heap and gets skipped as stale.

gotchas.text: Dijkstra needs every weight to be zero or more. With a negative link a finished node could still be improved, so 'finished' would be wrong. Use Bellman-Ford then.
Skip stale heap entries with: if popped time > best known time, continue. Without that check the answer is still right but the work can blow up.
Infinity is handy for 'unknown' and compares correctly, but JSON turns it into null. Keep it out of anything you display or serialise.
Nodes are numbered from 1. Make the arrays n + 1 long, or shift every index by one.
Use container/heap with an item type and call heap.Push(h, x) and heap.Pop(h). Calling h.Push or h.Pop directly does not restore the heap order.
math.MaxInt as infinity overflows if you add to it. Here we only add to a finished node's time, never to infinity, but a variant that relaxes from unreached nodes would break.

recap.key: Pop the smallest known time, skip stale entries, and push any neighbour whose time improved.
recap.complexity: Time O((V + E) log V). Space O(V + E).
moves: Set dist[k] = 0, others infinity, push (0, k)
Pop the smallest. Skip it if it is stale
For each link, if dist[u] + w < dist[v], update and push
Answer is the largest dist, or -1 if any is infinity
